claim: US artists employed part time had median annual earnings of only $20,380 in 2023, 3.4 times less than the $70,170 median for full-time employed artists, so the headline creative-occupation earnings figure describes only the full-time minority.
stance_target: The use of full-time creative-occupation median earnings as a benchmark for what people who make creative work typically earn
scope_conditions: United States only; American Community Survey 2023, constant 2023 dollars; nationally representative; earnings include wage-salary and NET self-employment income, so independent artists are captured; part-time defined as under 35 hours/week and/or under 50 weeks/year; the NEA cautions that part-time earnings are volatile
quoted_support: In 2023, artists employed part time typically earned 37 percent more than other (non-artist) cultural workers employed part time ($20,380 and $14,830, respectively).

claim: Part-time US artists earn statistically indistinguishably from part-time workers in general, meaning creative work confers no earnings premium at all once the full-time filter is removed.
stance_target: The claim that creative and creator occupations pay better than ordinary work
scope_conditions: United States only; ACS 2023; differences reported only where significant at the 95 per cent confidence level; part-time artists $20,380 versus all part-time workers $19,330
quoted_support: There were no measurable differences in earnings between part-time employed artists and all part-time workers in general.

claim: Median earnings of full-time US artists grew 5 per cent between 2015 and 2023 while all full-time workers gained 8 per cent, so creative occupations lost relative ground over the period the creator economy expanded.
stance_target: The position that growth in creative and creator activity has not translated into improving relative earnings for creative workers
scope_conditions: United States only; ACS 2015, 2019, 2023; constant 2023 dollars; full-time employed only; differences stated only when significant at p<.05
quoted_support: Between 2015 and 2023, the median annual earnings of full-time employed artists increased overall by 5 percent (from $66,910 to $70,170), while the median earnings for all full-time employed workers increased by 8 percent (from $56,860 to $61,170).

claim: Full-time US artists with a bachelor's degree or higher earn less than the general workforce with the same credential, even though artists as a whole out-earn all workers on the unconditional median.
stance_target: The claim that the creative-occupation earnings premium survives controlling for education
scope_conditions: United States only; ACS 2023; full-time employed; the NEA attributes the unconditional artist premium partly to artists' higher educational attainment
quoted_support: while artists with some college or an associate's degree earned more than all workers with similar education, those with a bachelor's degree or higher earned less than the general workforce.
numbers: $46,030 artists with less than high school
$38,720 all workers with less than high school

claim: Median full-time earnings across US artist occupations span 2.5x, from $39,230 for dancers to $99,630 for architects, and fell in 2023 for dancers, producers and architects.
stance_target: The position that 'creative worker' is not a single income class and occupation-level detail is required before any earnings claim is meaningful
scope_conditions: United States only; ACS 2023, constant 2023 dollars; full-time employed; 11 NEA artist occupations with some categories combined
quoted_support: Earnings for full-time employed artists ranged from $39,230 for dancers to $99,630 for architects.

claim: US administrative earnings data for artists counts only self-reported PRIMARY occupation, so anyone whose creative work is a secondary activity is structurally invisible in these statistics.
stance_target: The position that administrative occupational data cannot measure the part-time and side-hustle creator population that dominates content creation
scope_conditions: United States; American Community Survey methodology; the ACS asks only about the current or most recent job, or where there are two or more jobs the one with the most usual hours
quoted_support: "Primary occupation" refers to the kind of work a person does for pay most of the time. The ACS... asks only about the occupation corresponding to a respondent's current or most recent job or, if they have two or more jobs, the job with the most usual hours worked.
